identity/motivation.mdx: Built by Humans A few years ago, when I was building WorkInProgress from scratch, getting software out the door was an exercise in constraint. Every feature was a negotiation with time and resources. Today, those constraints have completely evaporated. Tools like Cursor, Claude Code, and the agents we interact with daily make the cost of writing software practically zero. It's a rapid shift. Companies are all-in on AI, and hundreds of billions are being spent to not fall behind. I have been thinking a lot about this shift, because when building becomes frictionless it becomes terrifyingly simple to waste our global resources building things that no one wants. We are entering a time where engineering velocity is no longer a bottleneck, and what has emerged is rather an importance of good judgment. This is why I am invested in product management today. To bring real value to real people. To design human-centric software that is unquestionably the best canvas for its users. In a world where you can spin up an entire product in a weekend, the only differentiation is the deep desire to fundamentally understand the people you're building for. Product excellence is developed through iteration, genuine curiosity about the user, and a rigorous approach to craft. It necessitates deep, human intentionality, and cannot be synthesized within the vacuum of a frontier-model. The next generation world-changing products will be constructed with AI, but they will be built by humans. I aim to create products that make a real difference for real people, ensuring that all things that I build are inherently, and undeniably, human. daine
projects/hyperscreen/readme.mdx: HyperScreen Project Manager · Amazon Capstone · Jan 2025 – Apr 2025 · Vancouver, BC AWS Vancouver postings routinely draw 750+ applicants , and AI application tools like Simplify and AIApply have made that number a trend rather than a spike. HyperScreen is the screening platform we built for their recruiters and hiring managers: applicants apply through a public portal, hiring managers set weighted scoring criteria per posting, and the system ranks the pool so first-round screening starts from a shortlist instead of a stack. The target was a 50% cut in screening time without trading away hire quality. What I owned I ran the requirements and the release plan: the terms of reference, the business requirements document, the project plan, and the module-by-module schedule the seven engineers built against. I assigned every task to two people . On a team where everyone has a full course-load, a member going dark during midterm season needs to be a risk mitigated from the start. Pairing every task made that survivable by design. Scope Four modules, each with its own design, dev and release dates: Module What it does Target release --- --- --- Applicant Public, no-auth job search and application with resume upload Feb 17 Hiring Manager Create postings, set and prioritize scoring criteria, evaluate and rank Feb 17 Recruiter/Admin Hiring-manager onboarding and accounts, master scoring criteria, launch evaluations Mar 14 Reporting Applicant counts, rankings, per-applicant detail, exports and visualizations Mar 14 Success metrics I defined the metrics against manual screening: 75% of applicants scoring above 80 should also be green-lit by first-round manual screening. 50% of HyperScreen hires still employed after one year. 50% reduction in average screening time, with all user actions responding in under 2 seconds Build Django 5 with DRF over PostgreSQL 17, a Next.js 15 / React 19 frontend in TypeScript and Tailwind, and django-q2 running resume evaluation as background jobs. Production is four Docker containers behind nginx, with the frontend, backend and database on a shared internal network. Resume parsing ran through PyMuPDF and python-docx, and scoring ran on a local Ollama model to keep inference free.
projects/oval-updates/readme.mdx: Oval Updates Solo build · 2026 – present A single Trump post can move billions in minutes. Oval Updates watches everything he and the White House put out, from Truth Social posts to press releases, and when something market-relevant lands it sends a Telegram alert with the affected tickers, a one-line trader's take, an estimated move probability, and a directional confidence. The problem The posts that matter arrive at all hours, buried in a firehose of ceremonial messages, political grievances, and rhetoric irrelevant to the market. They're easy to miss and hard to act on quickly. What an alert looks like Two numbers, not one Est. relevance asks whether the post moves anything at all. Directional confidence asks whether we know which way, given a move. Calibrated on 132 labeled events I hand-labeled 132 historical Trump and White House events with what the market actually did, by category, and derived per-category base rates that anchor the model's scoring rather than letting it guess. The pipeline Two stages, for cost as much as accuracy. A gate model scores every post and decides alert-or-skip, tuned for recall so it almost never misses a real mover. The analyst (Gemini 2.5 Pro) runs only on the 25% that survive, producing the tickers and direction in the alert body. Stack: TypeScript (ESM, Node 22) · trigger.dev v4 · Google Gemini ( 2.5-flash-lite gate + 2.5-pro analyst) · fast-xml-parser · Telegram Bot API. Honest limitations Estimating market direction is hard and unreliable. Oval Updates acts as an alert, rather than a trade signal.
projects/workinprogress/readme.mdx: WorkInProgress Co-founder & CEO · Jan 2024 – Apr 2025 · Vancouver, BC WorkInProgress is an internship platform built by students, for students and the small-to-medium companies that hire them. Traditional job boards turned applying into a numbers game. There was mass applications on one side, keyword-matching ATS filters on the other, and neither side trusting what comes through. WIP replaced that with a curated brokerage, optimizing for relationships over resumes on a pool of verified candidates. I co-founded it and ran it as CEO: the strategic, product and operational calls were mine, from the initial specs through fundraising. What I owned I ran product strategy, engineering delivery and go-to-market while leading a six-person cross-functional team of three developers, a designer and marketing. I also owned the fundraising and accelerator pipeline, writing the applications that took us to the finals of the UBC Startups SOAR Pitch Competition and within the top 5% of applicants for Summer YC '25 On the product side I ran 75+ customer discovery interviews — most of them at Vancouver Startup Week — to decode what recruiters actually struggle with, and turned those into the supply-side requirements that landed our first B2B partners. On the engineering side I worked directly on backend architecture, database modelling and analytics instrumentation. What the product does Four pillars, each aimed at a specific failure of the job-board model: Pillar Focus What it does --- --- --- Application caps Intent A hard quota on simultaneous active applications, so volume stops being a strategy Institutional pipeline Verification Mandatory .edu auth, mapping every profile to a verified school and grad date Behavioral profiling Fit Interpersonal and behavioral signals assessed before technical screening Recruiter tools Throughput Exclusive postings, candidate review, and async video screening The application cap is the one that defines the product. Every other board makes money when students apply more; capping applications is what makes a curated pool possible, and it only works if the postings on the other side are worth the spend. Traction 250+ waitlist signups from localized campus marketing, before a line of the platform was live — demand validated before it was built 0 → 500+ active users in 90 days on an email-led GTM, reaching 600+ total users including 200+ verified student profiles 31% month-over-month growth through the late-2024 launch cycle 580+ internship postings aggregated to bootstrap the demand side 5 recruiters onboarded into the pilot, securing 5 exclusive postings and our first paid corporate partner +15% signup conversion by segmenting drop-off cohorts in Google Analytics and Tag Manager, then interviewing users in the cohorts that leaked Build Node.js and Express microservices behind a TypeScript and React frontend, on PostgreSQL hosted on Render, with media in Google Cloud Storage and identity through Firebase Auth. What went wrong The two-sided cold start. We spent early cycles marketing to students and recruiters at once, which is the classic way to under-serve both. Recruiters were never going to show up before the candidates did, so we pivoted to an open internship board and a bi-weekly newsletter, pooled 600+ students on that alone, and used the pool to sell the partnerships. Overestimating B2B software adoption. The early product asked recruiters to adopt a new dashboard, manage API keys, and run candidates through a system outside their workflow. That's tool fatigue, not a value proposition. We abstracted the software away into a managed brokerage service, letting hiring managers offload filtering to us entirely. What I'd do differently We were students building for students, and on that side of the marketplace our instincts were right more often than not. We had no equivalent instinct for recruiters, and we never fully closed that gap. We should have been sitting with them: shadowing a hiring manager through an actual day, going where they go, learning the job rather than interviewing about it. What crowded that out was building. We made almost everything in-house when we could have paid for it, and the time that bought us in ownership it cost us in research. Being more capital-intensive earlier would have freed up capacity to find PMF in the recruiter segment. Recruiters live in Workday and Dayforce, and asking them to leave those systems for a second platform was a bigger ask than expected. A middleware layer might have been the answer: our application caps, institutional validation, and behavioral matching filtering candidates inside the ATS they already use, instead of asking them to come to us. --- There's a demo of the platform in this folder, along with photos of the founders and the team . The product itself is at wipnetwork.ca .
research/systopia/readme.mdx: UBC Systopia Lab Undergraduate research (CPSC 448) · Winter Term 1, 2025 · Supervised by Prof. Ivan Beschastnikh Formal modelling of Byzantine fault tolerant consensus — a specification of PBFT written in TLA+/PlusCal, verified with the TLC model checker, and structured so it can eventually be compiled into Go by PGo. Why bother formalizing a protocol A Byzantine fault tolerant system can maintain correctness even when participants lie: with n = 3f + 1 replicas, every correct replica must still reach the same decision while up to f deviate arbitrarily. However, the implementations of BFT protocols in standard programming languages is prone to concurrency bugs, race conditions, deadlocks, and shared-memory corruption, none of which standard testing reliably surfaces. Therefore, bridging the gap between formal theory and executable code using formal verification tools such as TLA+ and PGo is critical for blockchain consensus algorithms. TLA+ verifies the design mathematically; PGo compiles Modular PlusCal into runnable Go. Together they close the gap between a proof and the code that ships. How I built it Complexity layering — start with the smallest thing that can be verified, then add one source of complexity at a time, so each bug surfaces in the simplest model that can still produce it: 1. Echo protocol — single sender, single server. Establishes message passing, state transitions and correct termination. 2. Broadcast and leader logic — a designated leader replica broadcasting to its backups, the primary→backups pattern PBFT's pre-prepare phase needs. 3. The PBFT state machine — pre-prepare, prepare and commit as distinct phases, with the quorum arithmetic ( 2f + 1 ) that moves a replica between them. 4. Concurrent clients — the final model, PBFTconcurrentClient.tla , where multiple requests move through consensus interleaved. What verification actually caught Head-of-line blocking. Strictly sequential processing deadlocked: a replica awaiting a prepare message at the head of its inbox stalls forever if a slower peer's commit arrives first. The fix was architectural — a message pump that drains the inbox on arrival regardless of type into a local received log, with state transitions recalculated by monitoring that log rather than reacting to whatever arrived next. Shared-buffer corruption. A global msg struct used for message assembly let one replica overwrite another's payload mid-broadcast. Refactoring every temporary buffer into a process-local variable restored memory isolation between threads. Per-transaction state. With concurrent clients, a replica can be committed for sequence 1 while only pre-prepared for 2, which a single global state flag cannot represent. It became a sequence-indexed state map, so progress on one transaction can't disturb the finalization of another. What it proves, and what it doesn't Verification completed at 2 replicas and 2 clients in roughly seven minutes. At three or four, the reachability graph outgrew the machine and the TLA+ Toolbox exhausted RAM and crashed. That boundary matters, so it's worth stating: the model is a proof of the state machine and the concurrency logic, not of the Byzantine threshold, which needs N = 4 . It also exercises the happy flow rather than quorum progress under silence, omits the view-change protocol, abstracts cryptography to authenticated channels, and has no deterministic fault injection. Next Simulation mode and a bigger TLC allocation to reach N = 4 ; refactoring the specification into Modular PlusCal so PGo can generate a Go prototype; encoding the invariants from the original OSDI '99 paper; and a fault-injection harness that forces chosen replicas to misbehave on cue. --- The full report is in this folder, and the specifications are on GitHub .

system/prd.mdx: Portfolio OS — PRD It felt wrong to build a portfolio around product work and then not write the doc. Why Most portfolios are a list. Here's where I worked, here's what I shipped. I built this desktop so that you can understand how I think and how I approach problems. Also I wanted to build it. A few user stories Recruiter I want to see where someone worked and when without opening anything, so I can judge recency at a glance I want the newest thing first, so I'm not sorting by date in my head I want the resume in one click, because that's what I came for Hiring manager I want each role to open into actual artifacts, so I can check a claim instead of trusting it I want to look at organized information, so I can easily understand what supporting documents relate to what role Engineer I want two windows side by side to compare documents against each other I want a performant and responsive experience First-timer I want something telling me where to start, so an unfamiliar interface doesn't turn into a puzzle I want a normal page on my phone I want to the interface to be intuitive to me, so it's easy to navigate and learn How it's built Next.js App Router. The layout holds the desktop and taskbar permanently, so nothing unmounts when you navigate. Zustand owns the window list: id, title, type, minimized, maximized, z-index. Position stays local to each window as a motion value. Framer Motion handles dragging and animations. Content is MDX. All the prose styling lives in one file at the root, so the .mdx files are just writing. Labels and ordering are TypeScript. Two Vercel edge functions. /api/chat is the assistant — Qwen on Groq, streamed. Its prompt is built from data/tree.ts plus the documents a question matches. It points at nodes with the same tag the documents use. /api/contact is the Inbox — Resend, server-side. My address is an environment variable, not in the bundle. Both rate limited per IP. No database, no sessions, nothing to log in to.
